extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of 37,200 English multiple-choice math word problems annotated with operation programs using a new representation language. MathQA significantly enhances the AQuA dataset with fully-specified operational programs covering multiple math domain categories including geometry, physics, probability, gain-loss, and general domains.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.publisher: University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by taking problems from the AQuA dataset and carefully annotating them with formal operation programs using crowdsourcing. Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies, and these domains were used to prune the search space of possible operations to align with word problem text.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Math word problems sourced from the AQuA dataset (Ling et al., 2017), which contains over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level math word problems.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotation expansion: closely similar problems were identified using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance, numeric values were replaced with generic numbers, and annotations were expanded to cover more problems from the AQuA dataset.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems from AQuA were filtered to remove unsolvable problems (no words, sequence problems, requires options, non-numeric) and duplicates. Problems were categorized into domain categories (Geometry, Physics, Probability, Gain-Loss, General, Other) using n-gram frequency-based lexicon matching.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. They iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. Operation selection was sequential with hints (arguments, formula, explanation). Argument selection was restricted to numbers in the problem, constants, and previous calculations to prevent noise. Results were automatically calculated after each operation submission. Final programs had to include numbers from the problem and produce a result close to the correct numeric solution. Alignment validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank the operation program as valid.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Figure Eight (https://www.figure-eight.com) with a custom dynamic annotation platform
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% of annotations were valid, with 87% agreement between expert validation and crowdsourcing validation task. Validation accuracy across categories was 94.64%. For categorization, agreement between human annotators was 84% and their agreement with the model was 74.5%.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 validators per annotation (with 2 out of 3 agreement required for validity)
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The AQuA dataset from which MathQA is derived has statistical biases that models can exploit through pattern-matching. The categorization strategy can be slightly noisy due to use of only one mathematical interpretation for each domain-specific n-gram (e.g., 'square' or 'cube' may refer to geometry or exponential operations).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The representation language omits high-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely nonnumeric. Some problems require complicated or long chains of mathematical reasoning beyond current model capabilities. Categorization errors can occur due to ambiguous domain-specific terms. Sequence problems and high-order polynomial problems are currently unsolvable. Some problems have insufficient textual context or are erroneous.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing neural math word problem solvers (sequence-to-program models). The dataset is split 80/12/8% for training/dev/test.
